In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the outcome of patients with non-traumatic intracranial hypertension is determined by many factors, and the outcome is not predictable from the level of the intracranial or arterial pressure.
the minimum cerebral perfusion and the organ system scores are not useful as guides to prognosis, and that the outcome in patients with non-traumatic intracranial hypertension is unpredictable.

the prognosis in children with raised intracerebral pressure is poor, and that the minimum cerebral perfusion index and the organ system scores are useful guides to severity of disease and to prognosis, but that the outcome in children with raised pressure is not determined by the intracranial or systemic pressures alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intracranial hypertension is a marker of the severity of illness and the prognosis.
the minimum cerebral perfusion was the only factor which was significantly different between patients with good or poor outcomes.
the minimum cerebral perfusion was a better predictor of outcome than intracranial hypertension and organ system failure was a better predictor for mortality.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the minimum cerebral perfusion and intracranial hypertension pressure are important parameters in monitoring the patient with a non-traumatic coma and that these patients are at risk of developing multiple organ failure.
the minimum cerebral perfusion and organ failure scores can be used to assess severity of illness and predict outcome.
the organ system failure score and minimum cerebral perfusion index are good predictors of outcome in children with non-trauma-related coma.
